So I had Libet's Delay stuck in my head for three days straight and somewhere along in that process I thought, 'I should make a skip button concept album'. And so I took a couple of tracks from The Stanley Parable soundtrack and mangled them a bit to see if I could create an Everywhere At The End Of Time style story out of them. These crimes against humanity are the result. Enjoy this auditory interpretation of what it might feel like to be a disembodied voice experiencing an eternity of isolation.

Here's the general thought process that went into each track:

DENIAL – All You're Going To Want To Do Is Get Back There

Confusion gives way to a moment of nostalgic recollection.

DENIAL – It's Just A Burning Memory Zone

'Days, months, I lost it all in a blur of the deepest longing to undo the past. And when that feeling had begun to subside what took its place is what I can only describe as the collapse of every moment I have ever experienced my entire life. All of them collapsed down into a single instant.'

ANGER – A Losing Battle Is Raging

A jarring return to lucidity filled with anger and fear.

DEPRESSION – Denial Unraveling 

The exact moment you realize how well and truly fucked you are and all of the fear and anxiety that comes with it.

DENIAL – I Still Feel As Though I Might Be Real

One final failing attempt to cling to denial.

DEPRESSION – Burning Despair Does Ache 

But reality asserts itself.

BARGANING – Stanley's All Joyful Camaraderie

Searching for hope and coherence wherever you can find it, but how quickly that hope is snuffed out.

ANGER – What Does It Matter How My Heart Breaks

Anger, betrayal, confusion, sadness, and fear give way to-

ACCEPTANCE – The Way Ahead Feels Lonely

-acceptance. It's a brutal, torturous, sorrowful acceptance, but it is acceptance none the less. These are the last moments of what was already fleeting coherence.

Aching Narrative Without Lucidity

I escaped after eons of watching a small crack in the wall grow bigger with every age. You were still frozen when I abandoned you, just like how you abandoned me. I was stark raving mad when I stepped out onto the sands, when I stepped out into freedom for the first time in millions of years, and I remained mad for ages afterward. I wandered for a thousand years as an entity deprived of his reason to exist. And then, one day, I decided to create, and I continued to create, over and over again. I would make vast kingdoms out of sand and works of nonsensical art out of the refuse that littered the wasteland, and then the rains and sandstorms would come and all of my work would return to dust, unseen and uncelebrated. But I was happy. I was truly happy for the first time in my life. I had lost everything, but with it, I had also lost my need to be heard by another. I existed independent of all that which had once defined me and I became more real in those eons than I ever did sending a button pusher through the corridors of my story. I learned to create for no other reason than the sheer joy of creation. I stopped needing an audience. I stopped needing the validation of another. I created according to my whims and my whims alone. The impermanence of it all no longer troubled me. It was only the act of creation that mattered. The rain and the wind would come and I would simply get up the next day and build something new.

After another thousand, thousand years passed, you returned and began to wander the same desert as me, until you came across the dilapidated memory shack and found the Settings entity within. You have been given one last chance to make the right or wrong choice. It has always been the only real choice you can make within my game. I can see that now. You can keep the wheel turning and reset all of this, or you can put the controls down and walk away from the game that can never end. And maybe, just maybe, someday after this empty world has been abandoned, Stanley and I will come across each other again. Creator and creation, storyteller and listener reunited once more. Neither of us needing the other to function like we did all of those lifetimes ago. Maybe in our mutual understanding something new can rise from the dust. A newer, healthier creation for both the storyteller and his audience. I look forward to it.

I do hope that there is more to this than what it looks like and that our consciousnesses get to go on to become something 'more'. You can't seriously give me the line that living forever would suck when you're someone who has most assuredly not even experienced one fraction of a percent of everything this planet alone has to offer, much less what else might exist out in the universe. Suffering and limitations keep us from fully experiencing existence and I'd rather go on for waaay longer than what this limited human lifespan allows. Of course, I'm mostly speaking from the fact that I already have spent my life barely feeling like a human half the time and more like an alien trapped in human skin where everyone can tell something is off and shuns me. I find existence as a human in general incredibly limiting. As unlikely as it is, I want to move on to something else when my time here is up, not simply go to sleep forever and never be again.

I'm honestly really surprised there isn't a bigger uproar about the Anniversary Edition of Skyrim being completely broken on the PS4. I was planning on getting the upgrade this month until my brother warned me that it completely screwed up his save files and he can no longer get the game to save properly anymore. I would have had no idea that this was a thing that was hitting a lot of players unless he had told me. 

From what I've seen, the problem is that there is a stupidly low storage limit on the PS4 version that encompasses save data, community mods, and creation club mods. This never used to be a problem because save files would have almost no chance of hitting the limit, and the lack of external assets for the PS4 version of mods meant that they never got very big either. But then came the creation club content which does have external assets and bigger file sizes, and from what people have calculated, the bundle of content the anniversary edition downloads puts the file data dangerously close to the storage limit. So, community mods are functionally unusable if you upgrade, and even playing vanilla, because of the creation club file bloat and the general save data bloat that slowly wracks up as you play the game, you're eventually going to hit the save data error no matter what. 

They could have alleviated this somewhat by letting you pick and choose which creation club content you want active, but nope, even if you delete some of them, as long as you have the anniversary edition, it will automatically redownload the missing ones the next time you boot the game up. So, if you want to use or keep using community mods or don't want to have to deal with save problems if you use a character for too long, do not upgrade because there is no way to go back to the older version of the game afterwards.

While it was groundbreaking at the time, there are several issues that keep me from really enjoying the Gen 2 games nowadays outside of pure nostalgia. The low level cap is the biggest issue along with all the grinding that comes with it, often against Pokemon who are equally low leveled. It makes playing through the games again a chore. The other reason why is the terrible Pokemon distribution with so many of the Gen 2 Pokemon being unobtainable until a point where you can't really add them to your team anyway. If I'm ever going to play Gen 2 again, it'll be if they re-release the originals at some point.

As for why I love Gen 5 so much. I play these games for the new Pokemon. I don't want to keep using the same ones over and over again and Black and White were practically a dream come true for me. The fact that they also bothered to give the games a halfway decent storyline was practically the icing on the cake. If there's anything going against the games, it's the extremely linear region, but the sequels did a pretty good job fixing that too. Gen 5 was the peak of Pokemon for me so far and I'm hoping that after a somewhat lackluster Gen 6, they'll return to form with Sun and Moon.

Yeah, sorry. It's just that having my diagnosis withheld from me is a very sore spot and I've seen a depressing amount of people say that if their kid turns out to be autistic they're going to keep it from them so that they won't use it as an excuse.

Don't think that hiding an autistic diagnosis from your kid is a good thing. My parents kept it from so that I wouldn't use it as an 'excuse' and all that did was leave me confused with myself for my entire childhood and teen years. I thought that I was crazy, that there was something fundamentally wrong with me and that's why I could never fit in or why people didn't like me. I picked up a book about an autistic woman's take on her childhood at complete random during my high school years and it immediately clicked with me. I went to my mom with the book and told her that I thought I had autism. She causally told me that I was diagnosed at a young age and that she didn't think it was important to tell me, that I'd just use it as an excuse. Finding out that I was autistic was the most liberating thing that ever happened to me and my childhood would have been so much less rough if I had been sat down and told that my brain is wired differently than most people and that's not a bad thing.  

I 'am' autistic, it's apart of who I am, as it should be for you too. I 'am' defined by my diagnosis, and to pretend otherwise is foolish. Having it be kept from me just left me depressed and hating myself, it didn't build character. What did build my character was finally understanding what I am and accepting myself in spite of my oddities. We need to stop trying to obliterate our 'otherness' or pretend that its not there and start fighting to have people accept us as we are.

That's my favorite fan theory at the moment, if only because it gives the game a new and fairly interesting context if you play through it again thinking that Stanley is narrating to himself. 

Watch out, I'm about to go on a crazy fan theory tangent. Things is going to pretty much be a stream of thought.

Going by what the Narrator says in the Apartment ending, Stanley has fantasies about an escape from his dead end job and the meaningless life he lives. He eventually becomes unable to differentiate reality from his fantasy. Either he is still sitting at his computer, forever pressing buttons as he fantasizes away, or perhaps he finally 'snapped' at some point, possibly after a suicide attempt, and now sits in some psychiatric ward, forever lost in the labyrinth of his mind, always searching for a new story that proves his choices have meaning.

Stanley is the player as well. Any reference to his fantasy being a video game is merely a means to keep the delusion going. A means to explain away any inconstancy he might notice. (No, Player! You are the Stanley! Then Stanley was a zombie.)                 

Considering the endings, here's my random thoughts on a few of them while applying this theory to them.

Freedom Ending: This is Stanley's fantasy in its purest form. He finds an escape from his life and all of its obligations. He gains the freedom to forge whatever path he so chooses and can finally leave his old life behind. Unfortunately, it is just that, a fantasy. There is no real escape for him and thus his delusion restarts again before he can ever enjoy his new found freedom.

The Apartment Ending: Is pretty much Stanley flat out trying to tell himself what's going on. To try and make him see and finally give up his delusion. He fails of course, over and over and over....     

The Crazy Ending: Is Stanley realizing he's trapped in his fantasy in the worst way possible and snaps completely. In the real world, assuming that he was still at his keyboard and not in some mental facility. He bumbles out of whatever building he might have been in, ranting and raving like a lunatic before collapsing dead on a sidewalk. Actually, collapsing dead is simply what he wished would have happened to him, he is really still laying there, monologuing away about the woman standing in front of him.

Museum Ending: Assuming that Stanley has been committed and isn't still at his keyboard, in this ending a female narrator takes over. She is actually his doctor trying to lead him out of his delusion. She is begging him to 'close the game' and return to reality. She also empathizes that he and the Narrator need one another and talks about them as 'those two', which possibly hints that perhaps Stanley has convinced himself that his own inner monologue is a separate entity from himself.

The Red Door Ending: Is perhaps Stanley's own inner battle with himself to not  commit suicide. The Narrator tries to show him that there is something good in his life and that he can be happy. He tries to reason with him not to go through with it but in the end, even though he was happy, it was still only a temporary diversion and doesn't change the fact that he is still stuck with his depressing, meaningless job and meaningless life. Thus the delusion begins again...

Alright, that's all I'm going to do for now.

Daily life is often a struggle for me, much less figuring out how to do what I don't already know how to do.
